subject: Science
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 45 minutes × 11 periods = 495 minutes
Total: 11 periods · 8h 15min

periods.activity_title: Noticing the Moon in the Day Sky
periods.activity_description: Students examine the opening scenario of a Moon visible during daytime at a kite festival and identify what they already know and what puzzles them about the Moon's changing appearance. They record observations and initial questions about why the Moon's shape seems to change each night.

roles.role_description: Facilitates the opening scenario discussion and prompts students to articulate what they notice and what they find surprising about the Moon's appearance.
Record their prior observations of the Moon and formulate at least one question about why its shape appears to change.
Share their questions in small groups and compile a short list of what the group agrees it has noticed about the Moon.

time_bands.activity: Teacher presents the kite-festival scenario and asks students to describe any time they have noticed the Moon during the day or in an unexpected shape.
Students individually sketch the Moon shapes they recall from memory, labelling roughly when in the month they think each shape occurs.
Groups compare their sketches, identify agreements and disagreements, and compile a group list of observations and open questions.
Whole-class share-out of two or three open questions; teacher records them visibly to revisit across subsequent units.

periods.teacher_notes: This first unit orients students to the chapter's starting point — the visible Moon and its shifting shapes — before any explanation is introduced. Watch for students who conflate the Moon's phases with Earth's shadow; this misconception surfaces early and is directly addressed in a later unit. Keeping the class-generated questions visible throughout the chapter gives students a meaningful reference point as the arc progresses.
materials: Blank paper or notebooks for sketching
Whiteboard or chart paper for recording class questions

periods.activity_title: Mapping the Lunar Cycle: Phase Names and Positions
periods.activity_description: Students are introduced to the named phases — full Moon, gibbous, crescent, new Moon — and the two fortnightly arcs of Krishna Paksha and Shukla Paksha. They construct a circular phase-tracking diagram, placing phase names and sketched shapes around the cycle and annotating where in the sky and at what time of day each phase is easiest to spot.

roles.role_description: Introduces phase terminology through guided questioning and directs students through the construction of the phase-tracking diagram.
Create and annotate a circular phase diagram in their notebooks, recording phase names, approximate shapes, and viewing times.

time_bands.activity: Teacher draws a large circle on the board and names each phase position, connecting each to the waxing and waning terminology from the chapter.
Students construct their own phase-cycle diagrams, sketching the illuminated shape at each named position and noting the Sanskrit names Purnima and Amavasya.
Students annotate each phase with when it is easiest to observe — sunset for waxing phases, sunrise for waning phases — and note that the Moon rises about 50 minutes later each day.
Pairs check each other's diagrams against the chapter description and identify any phase they found hard to place.

periods.teacher_notes: Building on the previous unit's open questions, this unit gives students the vocabulary and structure to describe what they have been noticing informally. A common error is placing the full Moon at sunrise rather than recognising it rises near sunset and is opposite the Sun; prompt students to reason about where the Sun is when they sketch each phase position. The completed phase diagram becomes a personal reference students can use through the rest of this arc.
materials: Coloured pencils or markers for shading illuminated portions

periods.stage_label: Model and explain the cause of phases and eclipses
periods.activity_description: Students recreate Activity 11.2 using a ball on a stick as the Moon and a torch as the Sun, with the student's head representing the Earth. By rotating slowly and observing how much of the illuminated hemisphere is visible from the Earth position, students produce the same progression of phases they documented in the previous unit.

roles.role_description: Demonstrates the initial setup, then circulates to ask probing questions about what fraction of the illuminated side each student can see at each orbital position.
Take turns being the Earth observer while a partner holds the torch; each group member rotates through at least two orbital positions and sketches what they see.

time_bands.activity: Teacher demonstrates the setup — ball on stick, torch at one end of the room — and asks students to predict what they will see when the ball is directly between them and the torch.
Groups carry out the rotation activity, with one student as the Earth observer rotating and describing what they see, while another records which phase corresponds to each orbital position.
Groups compare their recorded orbital positions against the phase diagram from the previous unit to confirm the correspondence.
Brief whole-class discussion: why does the Moon shine at all? Students articulate that it reflects sunlight, not that it generates its own light.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit directly addresses the most entrenched misconception in the chapter: that Earth's shadow causes phases. Make sure students articulate that the phases arise from our changing viewpoint of the Moon's always-illuminated hemisphere, not from anything blocking sunlight. If a group gets confused, ask them where the dark region of the ball is at each position — the shadow is always on the far side from the torch, regardless of where the observer stands.
materials: Ball on a stick (or any round object on a pencil)

periods.stage_label: Model and explain the cause of phases and eclipses
periods.activity_description: Having established that phases are caused by changing viewing angles, students now learn the distinct causal mechanism of eclipses — Earth's shadow falling on the Moon during a lunar eclipse, and the Moon blocking the Sun during a solar eclipse. Students identify the precise orbital conditions (full Moon for lunar, new Moon for solar) and explain why eclipses do not occur every month.

roles.role_description: Explains the geometry of lunar and solar eclipses using a board diagram, connecting the explanation back to the ball-and-torch model from the previous unit.
Annotate a diagram showing the Sun, Earth, and Moon aligned for each eclipse type, labelling the shadow and penumbra and explaining in one sentence why eclipses are infrequent.

time_bands.activity: Teacher draws the Sun-Earth-Moon alignment for a lunar eclipse and a solar eclipse, asking students to compare these alignments with the full Moon and new Moon positions from their phase diagrams.

Students annotate their own diagrams, labelling Earth's shadow on the Moon (lunar eclipse) and the Moon's shadow on Earth (solar eclipse), and writing a sentence connecting each eclipse type to the phase on which it can occur.
Teacher explains why eclipses do not occur every full and new Moon — the Moon's orbit is slightly tilted relative to Earth's orbit — and students add this annotation to their diagrams.
Quick pair-check: each student explains to a partner the difference between what causes phases and what causes eclipses, using only their annotated diagrams.

periods.teacher_notes: The previous unit's model work makes this unit much easier: students have already held the ball at the full Moon and new Moon positions, so now they only need to understand when the three objects are exactly aligned versus slightly offset. The most common confusion here is thinking that the tilted orbit means eclipses are impossible — clarify that the tilt just makes alignment rare, not impossible. The pair-check at the close is a strong readiness signal: a student who can distinguish phases from eclipses in their own words is ready to move to the calendar arc.
materials: Notebooks with annotated diagrams from previous unit
homework: Draw and label the orbital positions for both a lunar and a solar eclipse, and write one sentence for each explaining why it occurs only on that specific phase day.

periods.stage_label: Derive calendar units from periodic celestial motions
periods.activity_title: Three Cycles, Three Units: Day, Month, Year
periods.activity_description: Students examine the three recurring astronomical cycles — Earth's daily rotation, the Moon's phase cycle, and Earth's annual revolution — and identify each as the basis of a calendar unit. Using the shadow-stick activity described in section 11.2, students reason about how tracking the shortest shadow each day measures the solar day.

roles.role_description: Guides students to connect each astronomical cycle to its calendar unit through questioning, and introduces the shadow-stick setup for measuring the solar day.
Discuss and record how each of the three cycles produces a natural, repeatable unit, then sketch the shadow-stick setup and explain what the shortest shadow indicates.

time_bands.activity: Teacher displays three observations — daily Sun movement, monthly Moon cycle, yearly return of seasons — and asks each group to match each observation to a time unit without being told the answer.
Groups discuss and record their reasoning, then draw a nested-cycle diagram (mirroring Fig. 11.8 from the chapter) showing day inside month inside year.

Teacher introduces the shadow-stick activity: students sketch the setup, explain that the shortest shadow marks solar noon, and describe how repeating this over consecutive days defines the mean solar day of 24 hours.
Each group shares one insight from their nested-cycle diagram; teacher consolidates the three units and their astronomical origins on the board.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit pivots from celestial phenomena to their practical consequence — the origin of time-keeping units — so briefly recall the phase and revolution work from the previous two units to help students see the continuity. Students sometimes confuse the sidereal month with the synodic (phase) month; at this stage keep the focus on the phase cycle as the basis of the calendar month and hold the sidereal distinction for a later unit. The nested-cycle diagram is a useful checkpoint: groups that can explain why the year is the outermost cycle have grasped the astronomical hierarchy.
materials: Ruler and a pencil for sketching the shadow-stick setup

periods.stage_label: Derive calendar units from periodic celestial motions
periods.activity_title: Why Lunar Calendars Drift: The 11-Day Problem
periods.activity_description: Students calculate and reason about the mismatch between the lunar year (12 × 29.5 days ≈ 354 days) and the solar year (365.25 days), discovering that the 11-day annual shortfall causes seasons to drift across lunar months over successive years. They evaluate why this drift matters for agriculture and identify the structural limitation of a purely lunar calendar.

roles.role_description: Poses the driving question — if the calendar is based on Moon phases, what happens to the seasons after several years? — and guides students through the arithmetic.
Calculate the lunar year length, find the annual shortfall, and project how many years it takes for the seasons to drift by a full month.
Discuss why seasonal drift is a practical problem and articulate the limitation in their own words before reporting back.

time_bands.activity: Teacher asks: how many days in a year of 12 lunar months? Students calculate 12 × 29.5 and compare with 365.
Students individually work through the drift: after 3 years, the lunar calendar is about 33 days behind; they reason about what this means for a harvest festival tied to a lunar month.
Groups discuss the agricultural implication — farmers who plant by the lunar calendar will find the seasons arriving at different lunar months each year — and draft a one-paragraph explanation.

Groups share their explanations; teacher summarises: a purely lunar calendar is internally consistent but seasonally unreliable, setting up the need for the solar and luni-solar solutions in the next unit.

periods.teacher_notes: The previous unit established the three astronomical cycles; this unit turns the month–year mismatch into an active problem students investigate rather than absorb. A frequent error is arithmetic: students may multiply 29.5 × 12 incorrectly, so circulate during the calculation phase. The goal is not just the number but the reasoning — students should be able to explain in a sentence why an 11-day shortfall compounds into a seasonal drift, not just state the figure.
materials: Calculators or scratch paper for arithmetic

periods.stage_label: Derive calendar units from periodic celestial motions
periods.activity_title: Solar, Luni-Solar, and the Indian National Calendar: Three Solutions
periods.activity_description: Students examine the structural design of the Gregorian solar calendar, the luni-solar calendar with its intercalary Adhika Maasa, and the Indian National Calendar, comparing how each solves the drift problem differently. They complete a structured comparison table and connect the Indian National Calendar's design to the recommendations of Meghnad Saha's Calendar Reform Committee.

roles.role_description: Provides the key data for each calendar type and guides students through the comparison table, highlighting where each calendar's design responds to the 11-day problem.
Complete the comparison table collaboratively, then each group explains one calendar type's solution to the rest of the class.

time_bands.activity: Teacher recaps the 11-day problem from the previous unit and poses: what are three different ways a calendar designer could solve this?

Groups complete a comparison table with columns for Calendar Type, Basis, How It Handles the 11-Day Problem, and Key Feature; rows cover Gregorian, luni-solar with Adhika Maasa, and the Indian National Calendar.

Each group presents one calendar row, explaining the solution mechanism; teacher adds the Indian National Calendar details — Meghnad Saha, 1956 start date, 22 March new year, Surya Siddhanta principles.
Students individually write one sentence connecting the tropical year and the leap-year correction to why the Gregorian calendar stays aligned with seasons over centuries.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit is the culmination of the calendar derivation stage, so students should arrive having articulated why the lunar calendar drifts. A common confusion is thinking the Indian National Calendar is luni-solar because it uses traditional month names — clarify that the names are borrowed but the structure is solar, based on the Surya Siddhanta and aligned to the spring equinox. The one-sentence close is a useful individual checkpoint before the arc moves to application.
materials: Pre-drawn or student-drawn comparison table template
homework: Using the comparison table completed in class, write a short explanation of why the Gregorian calendar requires both a leap year every four years and a correction that skips the leap year in most century years.

periods.stage_label: Apply astronomical reasoning to festivals and satellites
periods.activity_title: Festivals Anchored to the Sky: Phase-Based and Solar-Based
periods.activity_description: Students apply their understanding of lunar phases, luni-solar calendars, and solar calendars to explain why Indian festivals fall on different Gregorian dates each year or consistently on nearly the same date. They classify a set of named festivals by calendar type and trace each to its astronomical anchor — a specific lunar phase, a solstice marker, or an equinox.

roles.role_description: Introduces the festival set and guides students to use their calendar-type knowledge as the classification tool rather than cultural familiarity alone.
Classify each festival by calendar type, identify its specific astronomical anchor, and explain in one sentence why it does or does not occur on the same Gregorian date each year.

time_bands.activity: Teacher lists the festivals from section 11.3 on the board — Diwali, Holi, Buddha Purnima, Eid-ul-Fitr, Dussehra, Makar Sankranti, Pongal, Vaisakhi — and asks students to sort them without help into two groups: fixed Gregorian date and shifting Gregorian date.

Students complete an individual classification table linking each festival to its calendar type (lunar, luni-solar, solar sidereal) and its specific astronomical anchor (e.g. new Moon of Kartika, full Moon of Phalguna, winter solstice marker).

Teacher corrects common misclassifications and explains why purely lunar festivals such as Eid can shift across entirely different Gregorian months, while luni-solar festivals shift by less than a month annually.
Students revisit their classification table and add a brief correction note to any festival they initially misclassified.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit is the first in the application stage; students are now using the calendar machinery they built in the previous three units to explain real cultural phenomena. A frequent misclassification is placing Makar Sankranti in the luni-solar category because it is a traditional Indian festival — clarify that it follows a solar sidereal calendar and therefore falls on nearly the same Gregorian date annually, with a slow drift of one day per 71 years. Encourage students to explain their classification reasoning, not just state the category.

periods.stage_label: Apply astronomical reasoning to festivals and satellites
periods.activity_title: Spotting Satellites: Natural and Artificial Orbits
periods.activity_description: Students investigate artificial satellites as human-made extensions of Earth's orbital environment, exploring their altitude, orbital period, and observability with the naked eye. They plan a sky-watching session using Activity 11.4's guidance — identifying the best viewing window, what a satellite looks like compared to a star or aircraft, and how mobile apps or the ISRO website can predict passes.

roles.role_description: Introduces the key parameters of artificial satellite orbits (altitude ~800 km, orbital period ~100 min) and demonstrates how to use a satellite-tracking app or website to identify an upcoming pass.
Plan their observation strategy: identify the best time of day to look, describe what distinguishes a satellite from a star, and list two ISRO missions they would want to observe if possible.

time_bands.activity: Teacher connects the Moon as a natural satellite to the concept of artificial satellites, asking students what would change about an object's appearance if it orbited much lower and faster.

Students examine the satellite parameters from the chapter — ~800 km altitude, ~100-minute orbit, visible as fast-moving points just before sunrise or after sunset — and explain in writing why they are visible only in those windows.

Groups plan an observation session: they list the conditions needed (clear sky, just after sunset or before sunrise), describe how to distinguish a satellite from a star (steady motion, no blinking), and identify two ISRO missions from the chapter.

Groups share their observation plans; teacher adds the space-debris context — defunct satellites and the need for international cooperation — and asks whether this changes how students think about satellite launches.

periods.teacher_notes: The previous unit applied calendar knowledge to festivals; this unit broadens the application to artificial satellites, connecting human activity to the same orbital mechanics the chapter has been building. A common confusion is thinking satellites are visible because they glow — clarify that like the Moon they are visible only because they reflect sunlight, which is why the viewing window is just after sunset or before sunrise when the observer is in darkness but the satellite is still in sunlight. The space-debris discussion is a natural opening for students to reason about the long-term consequences of putting objects into orbit.
materials: Device with internet access (for satellite-tracking app demonstration, if available)

periods.stage_label: Trace celestial phenomena to periodic orbital motions
periods.activity_title: From Orbit to Observation: Explaining Three Phenomena from One Framework
periods.activity_description: Students are presented with three unfamiliar scenarios — an observer trying to predict when a crescent Moon will be visible, a calendar designer deciding when to add an intercalary month, and a satellite engineer explaining why a satellite is only visible at certain times — and must trace each to the underlying periodic orbital motion that governs it.

roles.role_description: Presents the three scenarios and facilitates a structured discussion that pushes students to cite the specific orbital motion at the root of each phenomenon, not just name the phenomenon.
Work through each scenario in their groups, producing a written explanation that explicitly names the periodic motion, its cause, and how it produces the observable phenomenon.

time_bands.activity: Teacher presents the three scenarios on the board without answers, asking groups to identify which orbital motion is relevant before attempting any explanation.

Groups write their explanations for all three scenarios, ensuring each explanation includes: the name of the periodic motion, its physical cause (rotation, revolution, orbital tilt), and the observable consequence.

Groups share their explanations; teacher draws out the common thread — all three phenomena trace back to periodic motions of Earth and Moon in their orbits — and highlights any explanation that successfully linked the causal chain completely.
Students individually note one scenario whose explanation they found genuinely difficult and one sentence saying where their reasoning stalled.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit opens the final stage of the arc, where students are asked to work across the whole chapter's content — phases, calendars, satellites — using a single explanatory framework of periodic orbital motions. Watch for groups that describe what happens correctly but stop short of naming why the orbital motion produces that outcome; the key benchmark is the causal chain, not just the description. The individual reflection note at the close gives you direct insight into which concepts need the most reinforcement in the final unit.

periods.stage_label: Trace celestial phenomena to periodic orbital motions
periods.activity_title: The Orbital Mechanics Behind What We See: A Chapter-Wide Causal Investigation
periods.activity_description: Students consolidate the chapter's central explanatory claim — that every phenomenon studied (phases, eclipses, calendar units, festival timing, satellite visibility) traces to periodic motions of Earth and Moon in their orbits — by constructing an annotated cause-and-effect map that explicitly links each phenomenon to its governing orbital motion.

roles.role_description: Facilitates the construction of the cause-and-effect map by posing targeted questions that surface gaps and ensure causal links are explicit rather than merely associative.
Construct the cause-and-effect map collaboratively, then each group presents one causal chain from orbital motion to observable phenomenon, explaining the mechanism at each step.

After group presentation, each student writes a two-to-three sentence answer to the chapter's opening question: why does the Moon's visible shape change each night, and how does this connect to how we keep time?

time_bands.activity: Groups begin constructing their cause-and-effect map, starting from the three periodic motions as root causes and branching outward to their observable consequences — phases, eclipses, day, month, year, festival dates, satellite visibility windows.
Each group presents one causal chain, explaining the mechanism linking orbital motion to the phenomenon; classmates add or challenge links on their own maps.

Students individually write their response to the chapter's opening question, drawing on the full map to trace the Moon's changing appearance to reflected sunlight and changing viewing angles, and connecting this to the month as a calendar unit.
Teacher asks one or two students to read their individual response; class identifies whether the causal chain — orbital motion to observation to timekeeping — is complete.

periods.teacher_notes: This closing unit asks students to do what the chapter's dissolution test requires: explain phases, calendars, and satellites by tracing each to the periodic motions of Earth and Moon. Students who stall often do so at the calendar link — they can explain phases but struggle to articulate that the month is the Moon's phase cycle measured, so prompt that specific connection if it is missing. The cause-and-effect map is the product of this unit; no prior unit's output needs to be present because each group builds it here from knowledge, not from a physical artefact.
materials: Blank paper or large notebook pages for cause-and-effect maps

coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students examine the Moon's changing visible shapes, assign phase names and terminology, and annotate a full phase-cycle diagram showing when each phase is visible in the sky.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can name all major lunar phases, place them in the correct sequence around the cycle, and state when each is easiest to observe in the sky relative to sunrise and sunset.

coverage_handoff.stage_label: Model and explain the cause of phases and eclipses
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students use a ball-and-torch model to derive the causal mechanism of lunar phases from reflected sunlight and changing viewing angles, then distinguish this from the shadow-based mechanism of lunar and solar eclipses.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can explain why the Moon's illuminated shape appears to change by citing the Moon's revolution and the changing fraction of its sunlit hemisphere visible from Earth, and can distinguish this mechanism from the shadow alignment that produces eclipses.

coverage_handoff.stage_label: Derive calendar units from periodic celestial motions
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students trace the day, month, and year to Earth's rotation, the Moon's phase cycle, and Earth's revolution; calculate the lunar-year drift; and compare how lunar, solar, luni-solar, and the Indian National Calendar each address the mismatch between these cycles.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can identify the astronomical basis of each calendar unit and explain how at least two calendar systems — including the Indian National Calendar — address the structural mismatch between the lunar month count and the solar year.

coverage_handoff.stage_label: Apply astronomical reasoning to festivals and satellites
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students classify Indian festivals by calendar type and trace each to its astronomical anchor, then apply orbital-mechanics reasoning to explain when and why artificial satellites are visible and what purposes they serve.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can classify a given festival by its calendar type and identify its specific astronomical anchor, and can explain why artificial satellites are visible only in the window just before sunrise or after sunset by connecting this to reflected sunlight and orbital altitude.

coverage_handoff.stage_label: Trace celestial phenomena to periodic orbital motions
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students construct cause-and-effect explanations for phases, eclipses, calendar units, festival timing, and satellite visibility by explicitly tracing each back to the periodic motions of Earth and Moon in their orbits.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can produce a causal explanation of any of the chapter's phenomena — lunar phases, calendar structure, festival date variation, or satellite visibility — by tracing it explicitly to the periodic orbital motions of Earth and Moon that govern it.

assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can name all major lunar phases, place them in the correct sequence around the cycle, and state when each is easiest to observe in the sky relative to sunrise and sunset.

competency.competency_text: Explain celestial phenomena — the phases of the Moon, the structure of calendars, and the role of artificial satellites — by tracing each to the observable periodic motions of the Earth and Moon in their orbits.

assessment_items.question_text: A student wants to observe a waxing crescent Moon. At which time and direction should the student look?

options.label: A
options.text: At midnight, looking directly overhead

options.label: B
options.text: At solar noon, looking toward the southern sky

options.label: C
options.text: Just after sunset, looking toward the western horizon

options.label: D
options.text: Just before sunrise, looking toward the eastern horizon

what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing this option indicates the student has confused the waxing crescent (which follows the Sun at sunset) with the waning crescent (which precedes the Sun at sunrise).
what_each_option_reveals.A: Choosing this option indicates the student has not connected phase position to the Sun's location and believes the Moon is visible overhead at midnight regardless of phase.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Choosing this option indicates the student does not recognise that the Moon is visible against a bright daytime sky only near the Sun, and has not linked the crescent phase to proximity to the Sun.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who struggle with directional language can be asked to point toward where the Sun sets and then reason about where a Moon that follows the Sun would appear. Students with strong cultural familiarity with Moon-sighting festivals may draw on that experience to anchor the answer.

assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can name all major lunar phases, place them in the correct sequence around the cycle, and state when each is easiest to observe in the sky relative to sunrise and sunset.

competency.competency_text: Explain celestial phenomena — the phases of the Moon, the structure of calendars, and the role of artificial satellites — by tracing each to the observable periodic motions of the Earth and Moon in their orbits.

assessment_items.visual_stimulus:
Phase | Bright portion visible | Indian name
Full Moon | Entire disc | Purnima
Waning gibbous | More than half, decreasing | —
Waning half | Half disc | —
Waning crescent | Less than half, near Sun | —
New Moon | None visible | Amavasya
Waxing crescent | Less than half, near Sun | —
Waxing gibbous | More than half, increasing | —
assessment_items.question_text: Refer to the table provided. A student observing the Moon each morning finds the bright portion growing smaller and the Moon appearing progressively closer to the Sun. Which sequence of rows in the table correctly describes what the student is observing, from the start to the end of this period?

options.label: A
options.text: Full Moon → waxing gibbous → waxing half → waxing crescent

options.label: B
options.text: New Moon → waxing crescent → waxing gibbous → full Moon

options.label: C
options.text: Waning gibbous → waning half → waning crescent → new Moon

options.label: D
options.text: Waxing crescent → waxing gibbous → full Moon → waning gibbous

what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing this option indicates the student has confused the waning arc (decreasing brightness, morning sky) with the waxing arc (increasing brightness, evening sky).
what_each_option_reveals.B: Choosing this option indicates the student has recognised the new Moon as an endpoint but reversed the direction of change, beginning rather than ending there.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Choosing this option indicates the student knows the full Moon is the starting point but has applied the wrong directional label, choosing waxing instead of waning for the shrinking arc.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who find the table unfamiliar can be directed to trace the bright-portion column from 'entire disc' downward and match that to the student's morning-sky observation. Students confident with the cycle can work from memory and use the table only to confirm their answer.

assessment_items.stage_label: Model and explain the cause of phases and eclipses
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can explain why the Moon's illuminated shape appears to change by citing the Moon's revolution and the changing fraction of its sunlit hemisphere visible from Earth, and can distinguish this mechanism from the shadow alignment that produces eclipses.

competency.competency_text: Explain celestial phenomena — the phases of the Moon, the structure of calendars, and the role of artificial satellites — by tracing each to the observable periodic motions of the Earth and Moon in their orbits.

assessment_items.question_text: In the ball-and-torch model of lunar phases, a student rotates slowly while holding a ball outstretched, with a torch representing the Sun. The student notices that regardless of where the ball is in the rotation, exactly half the ball's surface always faces the torch. What does this observation demonstrate about the Moon?

options.label: A
options.text: Earth's shadow falls on the Moon and covers a progressively larger portion of it each night, producing the sequence of phases.

options.label: B
options.text: One hemisphere of the Moon always faces the Sun and is always illuminated; phases arise because the observer on Earth sees different fractions of that illuminated hemisphere.

options.label: C
options.text: The illuminated portion of the Moon grows and shrinks because the Moon moves closer to and farther from the Sun during its orbit.

options.label: D
options.text: The Moon produces its own light from one hemisphere and reflects sunlight from the other, causing the alternating bright and dark phases.

what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing this option indicates the student has not accepted that the Moon only reflects sunlight and has invented a self-emission explanation to account for the bright hemisphere.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Choosing this option reveals the most common misconception in the chapter — that Earth's shadow causes phases — which the ball-and-torch activity directly challenges.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Choosing this option indicates the student has conflated distance variation with illumination variation, confusing an elliptical-orbit idea with the viewing-angle explanation.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who still find the model abstract can be invited to physically re-enact the rotation with a ball while shielding one side with a hand, observing the illuminated fraction before being asked to reason about it. Students who grasp the model quickly can be asked whether the same logic explains why half the ball is always lit even when the student is not rotating.

assessment_items.stage_label: Model and explain the cause of phases and eclipses
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can explain why the Moon's illuminated shape appears to change by citing the Moon's revolution and the changing fraction of its sunlit hemisphere visible from Earth, and can distinguish this mechanism from the shadow alignment that produces eclipses.

competency.competency_text: Explain celestial phenomena — the phases of the Moon, the structure of calendars, and the role of artificial satellites — by tracing each to the observable periodic motions of the Earth and Moon in their orbits.

assessment_items.question_text: Lunar eclipses occur only on full Moon days, yet a full Moon occurs roughly every 29.5 days and lunar eclipses happen far less frequently. What is the correct explanation for this difference?

options.label: A
options.text: A lunar eclipse requires the Moon to be at its farthest point from Earth in its orbit, which coincides with full Moon only occasionally.

options.label: B
options.text: Earth's shadow is too small to cover the Moon unless the Moon is unusually close to Earth, which does not happen every month.

options.label: C
options.text: Lunar eclipses are prevented most months because the bright sunlit hemisphere of the Moon faces away from Earth during full Moon.

options.label: D
options.text: The Moon's orbit is slightly tilted relative to Earth's orbit, so the Sun, Earth, and Moon are rarely in exact alignment even on full Moon days.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Choosing this option indicates the student has introduced the concept of orbital distance (apogee) as the controlling factor, conflating orbital geometry with the tilt explanation.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Choosing this option indicates the student accepts the shadow mechanism but misattributes the rarity to shadow size rather than orbital tilt, partially understanding the causal chain.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Choosing this option reveals a residual confusion between the phase mechanism and the eclipse mechanism — the student believes the illuminated hemisphere's orientation prevents eclipses rather than understanding that orbital tilt prevents the required alignment.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who find pure geometry difficult can be given a simple diagram showing two orbital planes at a slight angle and asked to point to where alignment is possible; this anchors the abstract tilt concept. Students confident with the geometry can be asked to extend their reasoning: on which other phase could a solar eclipse occur, and for the same orbital-tilt reason?

assessment_items.stage_label: Model and explain the cause of phases and eclipses
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can explain why the Moon's illuminated shape appears to change by citing the Moon's revolution and the changing fraction of its sunlit hemisphere visible from Earth, and can distinguish this mechanism from the shadow alignment that produces eclipses.

competency.competency_text: Explain celestial phenomena — the phases of the Moon, the structure of calendars, and the role of artificial satellites — by tracing each to the observable periodic motions of the Earth and Moon in their orbits.

assessment_items.question_text: A younger student tells you that the Moon looks like a crescent because part of it is in Earth's shadow. Using what you have learned from the ball-and-torch model, write a short explanation that corrects this idea and gives the actual cause of the crescent phase.
expected_elements: States that the Moon does not produce its own light — it reflects sunlight.
States that one hemisphere of the Moon always faces the Sun and is always illuminated.
Explains that a crescent phase occurs because the observer on Earth can see only a small fraction of the illuminated hemisphere, not because any shadow covers the rest.
Distinguishes this mechanism from Earth's shadow, which causes a lunar eclipse (not a phase).

SCR.inclusivity: Students who struggle with written explanation can be invited to sketch the ball-and-torch setup at the crescent position and annotate the diagram before writing. Students who find the written form easy can be challenged to add a sentence explaining why Earth's shadow produces a visually similar darkening but through a completely different mechanism.

assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can identify the astronomical basis of each calendar unit and explain how at least two calendar systems — including the Indian National Calendar — address the structural mismatch between the lunar month count and the solar year.

competency.competency_text: Explain celestial phenomena — the phases of the Moon, the structure of calendars, and the role of artificial satellites — by tracing each to the observable periodic motions of the Earth and Moon in their orbits.

assessment_items.question_text: A student calculates that a purely lunar calendar year (12 months of 29.5 days each) is approximately 354 days long. What is the consequence of using this calendar over several years?

options.label: A
options.text: The full Moon will occur on a different day of the week each month, making it impossible to predict festival dates.

options.label: B
options.text: The lunar calendar will align with the solar calendar after exactly four years, just as the Gregorian calendar does with a leap year.

options.label: C
options.text: The lunar calendar will gradually gain extra days each year, causing months to become longer than 30 days.

options.label: D
options.text: The seasons will gradually shift to different lunar months each year, so a month that falls in summer one year will eventually fall in winter.

what_each_option_reveals.C: Choosing this option indicates the student has confused the direction of the drift — the lunar calendar is shorter, not longer, than the solar year — and has not understood that the deficit accumulates.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Choosing this option indicates the student has shifted focus from the month–year mismatch to week-day variation, which is a different and unrelated issue.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Choosing this option reveals a direct confusion between the lunar calendar's 11-day shortfall and the Gregorian leap-year correction, treating two entirely different problems as the same mechanism.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who struggle with the abstract drift can be asked to project the shortfall concretely: after 3 years, the lunar calendar is about 33 days behind — that is more than a full month. Students strong in mathematics can be asked how many years it takes for the drift to equal a full year.

assessment_items.visual_stimulus:
Calendar Type | Basis of Month | Basis of Year | Method of Handling 11-Day Gap
Lunar | Moon's phase cycle (~29.5 days) | 12 lunar months (~354 days) | No correction; seasons drift
Luni-solar | Moon's phase cycle (~29.5 days) | Solar year (~365.25 days) | Intercalary month added every 2–3 years
Gregorian (solar) | Adjusted lengths (28–31 days) | Earth's revolution (~365.25 days) | Leap year every 4 years; correction at century years
Indian National Calendar (solar) | 30 or 31 days | Solar year; begins 22 March | Leap year aligned with Gregorian; Chaitra gains a day
assessment_items.question_text: Refer to the table provided. A calendar designer wants months to stay aligned with Moon phases AND seasons to remain aligned with the solar year. Which calendar type achieves both goals, and what is the mechanism it uses to do so?

options.label: A
options.text: Gregorian; it uses a leap year every four years to keep months aligned with both Moon phases and the solar year simultaneously.

options.label: B
options.text: Indian National Calendar; it adds a day to Chaitra in leap years, which simultaneously corrects the lunar phase count and the solar year length.

options.label: C
options.text: Lunar; it tracks only Moon phases and therefore both Moon phases and seasons are aligned by default.

options.label: D
options.text: Luni-solar; it retains Moon-phase months as the primary unit and periodically adds an intercalary month to keep the calendar year aligned with the solar year.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Choosing this option indicates the student has conflated the Gregorian leap-year correction with luni-solar alignment; the Gregorian calendar does not track Moon phases at all.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Choosing this option indicates the student has confused the Indian National Calendar (which is solar, not luni-solar) with a luni-solar system, likely because the month names are traditional.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Choosing this option indicates the student has not engaged with the 11-day problem and incorrectly believes a purely lunar calendar keeps the seasons aligned.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who find the table dense can be directed to read only the 'Method of Handling 11-Day Gap' column and identify which row addresses both goals explicitly. Students who are confident can be asked to explain why the Gregorian calendar cannot achieve luni-solar alignment no matter how the leap year is adjusted.

assessment_items.question_text: The Gregorian calendar adds a leap year every four years but skips it in most century years (1700, 1800, 1900) while restoring it in years divisible by 400 (1600, 2000). Explain why these two corrections — adding a day every four years and then removing it at century years — are both necessary to keep the Gregorian calendar aligned with the seasons over long periods.
expected_elements: States that Earth's revolution takes approximately 365.25 days, not exactly 365, so a quarter-day accumulates each year.
Explains that adding a leap day every four years corrects for this accumulation of four quarter-days.
States that 365.25 is not exactly correct — the tropical year is slightly less than 365.25 days — so a small over-correction accumulates over centuries.
Explains that skipping the leap year in most century years removes the over-correction.
Explains that restoring the leap year every 400 years (e.g. 2000) accounts for the residual difference, keeping the calendar accurate over very long periods.

SCR.inclusivity: Students who find the multi-step correction abstract can be asked to reason about just the four-year rule first, then be asked: if 365.25 days were not quite right either, what would happen over 100 years? This scaffolds the chain. Students who find this straightforward can be asked whether the Indian National Calendar uses the same correction mechanism and why.

assessment_items.stage_label: Apply astronomical reasoning to festivals and satellites
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can classify a given festival by its calendar type and identify its specific astronomical anchor, and can explain why artificial satellites are visible only in the window just before sunrise or after sunset by connecting this to reflected sunlight and orbital altitude.

competency.competency_text: Explain celestial phenomena — the phases of the Moon, the structure of calendars, and the role of artificial satellites — by tracing each to the observable periodic motions of the Earth and Moon in their orbits.

assessment_items.question_text: Makar Sankranti is celebrated on nearly the same Gregorian date every year, while Diwali falls on a different Gregorian date each year. What is the correct explanation for this difference?

options.label: A
options.text: Diwali falls on the full Moon of Kartika, and because the Gregorian calendar has a leap year every four years, full Moon dates shift slightly each year.

options.label: B
options.text: Makar Sankranti follows a solar sidereal calendar tied to the Sun's apparent position among stars, while Diwali falls on a specific phase day in a luni-solar calendar.

options.label: C
options.text: Makar Sankranti is based on a purely lunar calendar that happens to match the Gregorian calendar, while Diwali is based on a solar calendar that drifts.

options.label: D
options.text: Makar Sankranti is observed on the spring equinox, which falls on the same Gregorian date, while Diwali is calculated from the monsoon season, which varies.

what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing this option indicates the student has associated fixed-date festivals with the equinox rather than the correct solar sidereal marker, and has invented a monsoon explanation for Diwali.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Choosing this option indicates the student knows Diwali is lunar but misattributes the Gregorian date variation to the leap year rather than to the Moon-phase cycle drifting against the solar year.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Choosing this option indicates the student has reversed the classification entirely — applying 'lunar' to the fixed-date festival and 'solar' to the shifting one.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who are unfamiliar with the specific festivals can be directed to reason from the calendar-type properties: which type stays fixed relative to Gregorian dates? Connecting this to the sidereal versus tropical year distinction from the chapter is acceptable.

assessment_items.stage_label: Apply astronomical reasoning to festivals and satellites
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can classify a given festival by its calendar type and identify its specific astronomical anchor, and can explain why artificial satellites are visible only in the window just before sunrise or after sunset by connecting this to reflected sunlight and orbital altitude.

competency.competency_text: Explain celestial phenomena — the phases of the Moon, the structure of calendars, and the role of artificial satellites — by tracing each to the observable periodic motions of the Earth and Moon in their orbits.

assessment_items.question_text: Artificial satellites orbiting at about 800 km altitude are best spotted just after sunset or just before sunrise. Why are they not visible in the middle of the night, even though they are continuously orbiting?

options.label: A
options.text: At midnight, the satellite is on the opposite side of Earth from the observer and therefore below the horizon.

options.label: B
options.text: In the middle of the night the satellite is in Earth's shadow and receives no sunlight to reflect toward an observer on the ground.

options.label: C
options.text: Satellites slow down and descend to lower orbits in the middle of the night because the Sun's radiation no longer provides thrust.

options.label: D
options.text: The satellite's own light source is switched off during the night to conserve power, making it invisible to the naked eye.

what_each_option_reveals.C: Choosing this option indicates the student has a misconception about satellite propulsion, believing sunlight provides continuous thrust rather than understanding that satellites orbit by inertia.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing this option indicates the student has attributed satellite visibility to an active light source rather than to reflected sunlight — the same misconception addressed for the Moon earlier in the chapter.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Choosing this option indicates the student has confused the viewing geometry with an orbital-position argument; at ~800 km altitude a satellite is visible across a wide arc of the sky and is not blocked by Earth at midnight.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who find the geometry difficult can be asked to draw a simple diagram: the satellite's orbit as a circle, Earth in the centre, and the Sun far to one side — then shade Earth's shadow cone and reason about when the satellite enters it. Students who immediately grasp the shadow argument can be asked to predict at what orbital altitude the shadow-window would effectively disappear.

assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can classify a given festival by its calendar type and identify its specific astronomical anchor, and can explain why artificial satellites are visible only in the window just before sunrise or after sunset by connecting this to reflected sunlight and orbital altitude.

assessment_items.question_text: Eid-ul-Fitr is celebrated after sighting the crescent Moon at the end of Ramazan. Explain why Eid-ul-Fitr can fall in entirely different seasons of the Gregorian year in different years, while Dussehra, celebrated on the tenth day of Ashwina, shifts less dramatically across Gregorian dates.
expected_elements: States that Eid-ul-Fitr follows a purely lunar calendar — months are based solely on the Moon's phase cycle.
Explains that a lunar year of 12 months is approximately 354 days, about 11 days shorter than the Gregorian solar year.
Explains that this 11-day annual shortfall accumulates so that over about 33 years, Eid-ul-Fitr cycles through all seasons of the Gregorian year.
States that Dussehra is a luni-solar festival — its calendar uses lunar months but adds an intercalary month every 2–3 years to correct the drift.
Explains that the intercalary correction keeps luni-solar festival dates within roughly the same season each year, preventing a full seasonal shift.

SCR.inclusivity: Students who find it difficult to begin can be asked to write down the calendar type for each festival first before attempting an explanation. Students who are confident can be challenged to estimate approximately how many years it takes for Eid-ul-Fitr to complete one full seasonal cycle through the Gregorian year.

assessment_items.stage_label: Trace celestial phenomena to periodic orbital motions
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can produce a causal explanation of any of the chapter's phenomena — lunar phases, calendar structure, festival date variation, or satellite visibility — by tracing it explicitly to the periodic orbital motions of Earth and Moon that govern it.

competency.competency_text: Explain celestial phenomena — the phases of the Moon, the structure of calendars, and the role of artificial satellites — by tracing each to the observable periodic motions of the Earth and Moon in their orbits.

assessment_items.question_text: A student claims: 'All the phenomena studied in this chapter — the Moon's phases, the length of a month in every calendar, and when artificial satellites are visible — ultimately trace back to one single idea: celestial bodies move in periodic orbits, and we observe the consequences of those orbits from a moving Earth.' Evaluate this claim. Is it valid, partially valid, or invalid? Justify your answer by referring to at least two specific phenomena from the chapter.

options.label: A
options.text: Invalid; the Moon's phases are caused by Earth's shadow, which is not an orbital phenomenon, and calendar months are cultural conventions with no direct astronomical basis.

options.label: B
options.text: Partially valid; phases and calendar months trace to orbital motion, but satellite visibility is governed by the satellite's power supply and antenna direction rather than by orbital position.

options.label: C
options.text: Partially valid; phases trace to orbital motion, but the length of the calendar year traces to Earth's axial tilt rather than to its orbital revolution.

options.label: D
options.text: Valid; lunar phases arise from the Moon's orbital revolution changing which fraction of its sunlit hemisphere is visible from Earth, and the calendar month is derived from the 29.5-day periodicity of that same phase cycle.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Choosing this option indicates the student has not connected satellite visibility to reflected sunlight and orbital position, retaining a technology-based rather than orbital explanation for visibility.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Choosing this option indicates the student has confused the cause of seasons (axial tilt) with the cause of the year's length (orbital revolution), partially dismantling the chapter's unifying claim.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Choosing this option reveals persistent retention of the Earth's-shadow misconception for phases, combined with a view that calendars are purely conventional — the most fundamental misunderstanding the chapter is designed to correct.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who find evaluating a claim difficult can be directed to test the claim against one phenomenon at a time rather than trying to evaluate it globally. Students who grasp the evaluation quickly can be asked to identify any phenomenon in the chapter that might require a qualification or caveat to the student's claim.

assessment_items.question_text: If the Moon's orbital period were exactly 30 days instead of 29.5 days, and Earth's revolution were exactly 360 days instead of 365.25 days, which of the following consequences would follow?

options.label: A
options.text: A lunar year of 12 months would be 360 days, perfectly matching the solar year, eliminating the need for any intercalary correction in luni-solar calendars.

options.label: B
options.text: Lunar eclipses would occur every full Moon because the Moon's longer orbital period would bring it into exact alignment with Earth and the Sun every month.

options.label: C
options.text: The Gregorian leap-year rule would no longer be needed because the solar year would already be a whole number of days.

options.label: D
options.text: The Moon would complete more than 12 phase cycles per year, making the lunar year longer than the solar year and requiring months to be removed periodically.

what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing this option indicates the student has misread the hypothetical — a 30-day period gives exactly 12 months in 360 days, which is fewer phase cycles per year than reality, not more.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Choosing this option indicates the student has confused the period of the Moon's orbit with the orbital tilt as the factor controlling eclipse frequency; eclipse frequency depends on alignment geometry, not orbital duration.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Choosing this option is partially correct — it is true that the leap year addresses the fractional day — but it is not the best answer because it ignores the more fundamental consequence: the month–year match. Students who choose this have analysed only half the hypothetical.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who find the hypothetical difficult can be directed to calculate 12 × 30 and 12 × 29.5 and compare both with the corresponding solar-year figures before attempting to reason about the consequence. Students who are confident can be asked to identify one aspect of the calendar system that this hypothetical would NOT change.

assessment_items.question_text: A friend who missed the chapter says: 'I don't see why astronomers and calendar-makers are connected. Stars and planets are one thing; counting days and months is just maths.' Write a response that traces at least three specific phenomena from this chapter — choosing from lunar phases, the origin of the calendar month, the design of luni-solar versus solar calendars, festival date variation, and satellite visibility — back to the periodic orbital motions that govern them, and use this to show your friend why the calendar is fundamentally astronomical.
look_for: Correctly identifies and names at least three specific phenomena from the chapter's content.
For each phenomenon, explicitly states the periodic orbital motion responsible — not just names the phenomenon.

Constructs a causal chain linking the orbital motion through the observable consequence to the calendar or timekeeping implication (e.g. Moon's revolution → changing viewing angle → phase cycle → 29.5-day month → calendar month).
Distinguishes between at least two different orbital motions (e.g. Earth's rotation vs. Earth's revolution vs. Moon's revolution) rather than attributing everything to a single motion.
Addresses the friend's implicit claim directly — that calendar arithmetic is separate from astronomy — with evidence from the chapter.

ECR.inclusivity: Students who find extended writing difficult can be invited to construct a brief annotated list of three phenomena with one causal sentence each before developing the prose. Students who write with ease can be challenged to include the eclipse geometry as a fourth phenomenon and explain why eclipses are not monthly despite the monthly full Moon.

assessment_items.visual_stimulus:
Scenario | Observable phenomenon | Periodic motion responsible | How the motion produces this phenomenon | Calendar or practical consequence
A new Moon is observed in the sky on the evening marking the start of Ramazan | Crescent Moon visible at sunset | | |
A harvest festival is always celebrated in the same season each year despite using lunar month names | Festival stays in the same season | | |
An artificial satellite appears as a moving point of light just after sunset but cannot be seen two hours later | Satellite visible at dusk, invisible at midnight | | |
The shadow cast by a vertical stick is shortest at the same clock-time each day, but that shortest length varies with the season | Daily shadow minimum; seasonal variation in length | | |
assessment_items.task: Refer to the table provided. Each row describes a real observable phenomenon. For each scenario: (1) identify the periodic orbital motion responsible, (2) explain how that motion produces the observable phenomenon, and (3) state the calendar or practical consequence that follows from it.
assessment_items.scaffold: Use the orbital motions you have studied — Earth's daily rotation, the Moon's revolution around Earth, Earth's annual revolution around the Sun — as your starting points. For each row, trace the chain: which motion → what it causes to change → what the observer sees → why this matters for timekeeping or practical life.
format_of_output: Completed table with all three columns filled for each of the four rows

A one-paragraph summary (3–4 sentences) connecting all four scenarios to the chapter's central idea: that the periodic motions of Earth and Moon in their orbits are the astronomical foundation of how we keep time.

OPEN_TASK.format_type: Data interpretation task (provided table or graph)
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The table presents four distinct scenarios drawn from across the chapter — festivals, satellites, shadows, and phases — requiring the student to apply the chapter's unifying causal framework to each in turn, which is the most direct demonstration of the final stage implied LO.
OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: A complete response demonstrates that the student can trace any observable phenomenon from this chapter back to the specific periodic orbital motion responsible for it, construct the causal chain from motion through observation to consequence, and see all phenomena as expressions of the same underlying astronomical framework.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The scaffold directs students to begin from the orbital-motion vocabulary rather than from the observed phenomenon, which forces the causal direction the LO requires. Students who start from the phenomenon and work backward are demonstrating the same cognitive operation and should not be penalised for the direction of their reasoning.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong responses: correctly identify a distinct orbital motion for each row (not one motion for all four); construct a complete causal chain for at least three rows; the summary paragraph uses the causal language of the chapter (revolution, rotation, phase cycle, reflection) rather than re-describing the phenomena. Weak responses: list the observed phenomenon again rather than the motion responsible; use 'the Earth moves' as a complete causal explanation without specifying which motion; leave the calendar-or-practical-consequence column blank or vague.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who find the table format constraining can be permitted to answer each row as a short paragraph. Students who complete the table quickly can be asked to add a fifth row of their own — a festival or observation not in the table — and apply the same causal framework to it.
